articles.title: Noor Ben Yessef: “7 de cada 10 comentarios en mis redes son insultos racistas”
articles.standfirst: La periodista hispanomarroquí pasa a formar parte del equipo de 'La Séptima'
articles.summary: La periodista hispanomarroquí pasa a formar parte del equipo de 'La Séptima'
articles.body: La Séptima todavía no ha comenzado sus emisiones y ya tiene etiqueta. “Los rojos”, “sanchistas” o “Tele Pedro” son algunos de los calificativos que, según Noor Ben Yessef, ha recibido la nueva cadena antes incluso de echar a andar. La periodista será uno de sus rostros visibles y tendrá su propio programa en la franja de tarde-noche. En 'Otra Ronda', el programa de Radio MARCA que presenta y dirige Carlos Vicente 'Chitu', habló sobre su nueva aventura, su salida de Antena 3 y los prejuicios que ha tenido que afrontar durante su carrera. “Nacemos con la idea de crear sinergia, incluso con otras teles”, explicó Ben Yessef sobre el proyecto. La periodista remarcó que La Séptima será una cadena “100% de financiación privada” y quiso desligar la mirada progresista que reivindica el proyecto de una adscripción partidista. “Ser progresista no es ser partidista”, afirmó. Ben Yessef reconoce que la nueva cadena nace rodeada de prejuicios. “Nacemos con múltiples prejuicios. Los rojos, sanchistas también... Tele Pedro también nos han llamado”, relató durante la entrevista. Frente a esas etiquetas, defiende que la intención de La Séptima es apostar por la pluralidad. “Yo espero que venga Ayuso, espero que venga Almeida, espero que venga Santiago Abascal, espero que vengan todos, sinceramente”, aseguró. La periodista incluso plantea contar públicamente qué dirigentes rechacen las invitaciones de la cadena. “Contaremos también a quienes hayan rechazado la invitación, porque no queremos que nos acusen de no ser plurales cuando nacemos con esa idea clara de ser plurales nosotros”, explicó. Ben Yessef defiende además que el proyecto no pretende ocultar su mirada progresista. “Nosotros nacemos con la idea del progresismo, que no significa nada más y nada menos que aumentar derechos sociales, aumentar libertades y mantener las igualdades”, afirmó. La llegada a La Séptima se produce después de su salida de Antena 3, donde desarrolló buena parte de su carrera profesional. Ben Yessef explicó que dejó la cadena en enero, aunque la salida se hizo pública en mayo, y que la decisión estuvo relacionada inicialmente con cuestiones personales y laborales. “Me fui en enero, aunque lo hice público en mayo”, explicó. La periodista señaló que llevaba tiempo trabajando como freelance y que había recibido ofertas, pero ninguna como la de La Séptima. La propuesta llegó de José Miguel Contreras, quien le preguntó cuál era su sueño profesional. “Se lo conté y ya rápidamente me ofreció un programa con esas líneas y esas bases en las que yo me siento cómoda”, recordó. Ben Yessef también quiso desmentir las teorías que apuntaban a que su salida de Antena 3 estaba relacionada con diferencias con la línea editorial de la cadena o que su incorporación a La Séptima estaba preparada de antemano. “Ha sido todo tan inesperado y tan orgánico que me emociona porque no sabes lo que la vida te va a deparar cuando decides ser valiente”, aseguró. Antes de dar el salto a su nuevo programa de televisión, Ben Yessef ha desarrollado también su faceta de entrevistadora a través de 'Acento Noor', un podcast en el que ha conversado con perfiles muy diferentes, desde representantes de la política como Yolanda Díaz hasta deportistas como Marcos Llorente. Precisamente, esa capacidad para sentarse frente a personas con posiciones diferentes es una de las características que reivindica de su manera de hacer periodismo. “Me gusta conversar con personas que tienen pensamientos diferentes al mío”, explicó en Radio MARCA. Y puso como ejemplo el tipo de entrevistas que le gustaría hacer: “Yo soy una periodista y persona en general que me gusta conversar con personas que tienen pensamientos diferentes al mío”. Para Ben Yessef, esa pluralidad no siempre está presente en los medios y considera necesario que exista tanto diversidad entre los entrevistados como entre los propios periodistas. La periodista también habló de una realidad mucho más personal: los comentarios racistas que recibe en redes sociales. Según explicó, en algunas publicaciones llega a encontrarse con que “7 de cada 10” comentarios son racistas. “Uno te dice qué bien lo has hecho, otro qué guapa vas... y otro ‘vete a tu país’ o ‘p**** mora’”, relató. Aseguró que este tipo de comentarios se han incrementado en los últimos meses, pese a que su identidad no ha cambiado: “Tenía el mismo padre marroquí y la misma madre española y me definí igualmente como hispana marroquí”. Ben Yessef reivindica precisamente esa doble pertenencia. “Yo me defino como hispana marroquí porque tengo mucho arraigo social, cultural y familiar con Marruecos y soy española, sevillana”, explicó. Una experiencia que conecta con otra de las ideas que ha desarrollado durante su carrera: la necesidad de ocupar espacios sin tener que justificar constantemente por qué se está en ellos. “En esta profesión nos juzgan por todo”, afirmó. “He aprendido en este tiempo eso”. Ahora afronta una nueva etapa con La Séptima. “Es un sueño lo que estoy viviendo”, reconoció.

articles.body: Wynonna Judd is finally telling her story – even the parts that may be painful for her family to hear. articles.title: Conan O'Brien compares declining late-night TV landscape to Detroit
articles.summary: Comedian Conan O'Brien compared late-night TV's decline to Detroit and discussed his transition into podcasts during an interview at Bloomberg Screentime.
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — Veteran funnyman Conan O'Brien spoke in blunt terms about what he's observed in the late-night television landscape Wednesday, comparing its decline to Detroit. Speaking at Bloomberg Screentime 2026, O'Brien was asked by Bloomberg's Ashley Carman whether he believed late-night TV "made sense economically," prompting him to look back at the evolution of late-night from its origins. The former NBC host first pointed to how networks in the late 1940s would go off the air at 10:30 and just have the American flag and music playing overnight, until his ex-employer was the first to fill the empty airtime with more television. JIMMY KIMMEL ERUPTS OVER QUESTIONS ABOUT LATE-NIGHT TV'S RELEVANCE IN STAR-STUDDED 'LATE SHOW' EPISODE "And my analogy has always been, you own a nice house, kind of like 'It's a Wonderful Life' house, you fix it up, the kids live there, it's the nice old drafty Victorian, and then you realize, hey, there's an attic," O'Brien said. "What you do is you go up there, and you just put down some basic flooring and put some beds in there, and suddenly you have all this room you didn't know you had." "That's what networks did," he continued. "They found room that was not being used. NBC, in particular, capitalized on it. You have an early show, then you have Steve Allen, then Jack [Paar], then Johnny Carson, and you're off and running." He said late-night TV quickly became "a giant machine that fires out cash" and remained so when he began hosting "Late Night with Conan O'Brien" in 1993. "And then I saw over my 17 years with NBC ... I started to see, oh, this is really changing. This is really changing," O'Brien said. "They're asking us to be much more cost-conscious. And it was for a good reason, which is that HBO, Cinemax, these are the things [that] are coming up. There's more networks — instead of one late-night show, 'The Tonight Show,' there's now 'Tonight Show' and there's David Letterman's show, then there are other shows." COLBERT LASHES OUT AT CBS, SAYS CANCELLATION ‘REINFORCED A NARRATIVE’ OF ‘KNEE BENDING’ TO TRUMP "It's a little like Detroit and automobiles. Like, the things just started to change, and you can get really upset about it," he continued. "But then streamers come along. And then I'm not even mentioning the internet. For years, we were working really hard to do something innovative and creative at night. Now you're competing with how many people in America are posting videos every day, or worldwide. Hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of millions of people are making funny videos." "If you do the math, nine of them are going to be one of the funniest things you've ever seen. Those come out every day. That's what you're competing against." O'Brien spent decades on late-night television between his stints on NBC and TBS before transitioning into podcasts; he now hosts "Conan O'Brien Needs a Friend." TBS ultimately scrapped its late-night programming in 2022 following the cancellation of "Full Frontal with Samantha Bee." Earlier this year, CBS pulled the plug on "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert," replacing it with Byron Allen's syndicated comic talk show "Comics Unleashed." "The Late Show" reportedly was losing CBS $40 million a year and had been running on a whopping $100 million budget per season. articles.title: Kavan: What's Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar got to do with an opera?
articles.summary: The moment you hear the word opera, you picture a grand musical presentation with fine costumes and trained singers performing for an audience that has
articles.body: The moment you hear the word opera, you picture a grand musical presentation with fine costumes and trained singers performing for an audience that has paid a sizeable amount on the tickets. But Kavan turns this identity upside down. "The common perception of an opera is that it's grand and meant for the elite. We wanted to question this perception. An opera can be staged by anyone. Through Kavan, we are doing it in our style with the tools available to us," says Dhammarakshit Randive, one of the performers.Ambedkarite by thought, not necessarily by birthAn Ambedkarite opera, Kavan will make its Pune debut today. The theatrical presentation predominantly uses music – rap, folk and electronic - but is a mix of acts and audio-visuals that are connected through Sudesh Jadhav's story. "At its heart this is a story of love and friendship," says Randive, highlighting the uniting power of both in a divisive world. Kavan has its roots in the shahiri tradition of folk performances, the writings of which have long highlighted social issues. Elaborating on that, Randive says, "What Shahirs wrote was not something to just read. It was meant to be performed as well. Kavan gets its name from this tradition, and this is our way of carrying that legacy forward." Randive, who has been involved in the Ambedkarite cultural movement for over a decade, also specifies that this is an Ambedkarite opera because everyone involved identifies with the thought process. "Not everyone in our team is born a dalit," he explains, adding, "But everyone identifies with Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar's thoughts on caste bias, the Indian Constitution and more. One becomes an Ambedkarite by thought, irrespective of gender, religion or anything else. That's also the kind of diversity that we have in our collective."The combination of politics and art stands out for me in Kavan. And to get to work with performers from Yalgaar who are politically, theatrically and musically at the top of their game is an honour for any directorLove and friendship as binding factorsThrough Yalgaar Sanskrutik Manch and Nalanda Arts Studio, Kavan is tapping into new audiences. While the collective has been doing folk and street performances across Maharashtra for a while, this is their first tryst with proscenium theatre. The opera had its opening show at Prithvi Theatre and travelled to Goa and Karnataka as well. "We're glad to be using this platform to take our thoughts to a newer set of people, and not limiting them to internal discussions within the collective. It's not propaganda. In fact, the core themes of love and friendship act as binding factors in a world divided in the name of religion, cast views and what not," says Randive. Abhishek Majumdar, the director of the play, adds, "As a society we don’t want to give up the privileges we have, and because of that we don't understand that what makes us strong is our ability to create equality. That is the idea of society that Babasaheb Ambedkar created the India Constitution with and it’s what we signed up for. I hope even those who disagree with the Ambedkarite view are able to have a conversation after watching Kavan.”People often stay away from political or critical theatre presentations today. Our approach is that we will present our thoughts no matter what. Hopefully, it will encourage more people to think beyond their limited world viewBOXWhat is Kavan?In a rapidly changing India, young Bejul and those around him navigate their dreams, desires, dilemmas while also negotiating caste and class. An operatic satire, written and performed fully in poetry and songs about young Ambedkarite experiences, Kavan attempts to encapsulate the rapidly changing India we see around ourselves - a country with mounting ambition, full of contradictions. Where do we go when the boundaries between right and wrong, sacred and profane, personal and universal are blurred? The opera has music and songs by BamBoy and MD Pallavi. It features Siddharth Pratibhawant, Pravin Mukta, Priypal Dashantee, Dhammarakshit Randhive, Amruta Todarmal and Apurva Kadam on stage.As artistes, it’s equally important to watch the performances of other artistes and experiencing interdisciplinary presentations. It changes our perceptions and helps us grow. articles.title: 'Funk', filme de ficção estrelado pela atriz Duda Santos como MC Sabrina, estreia no Brasil no Festival do Rio | G1
articles.body:
A atriz Duda Santos interpreta a jovem funkeira MC Sabrina, protagonista do filme de Aly Muritiba — Foto: Vincent Rosenblatt / Still do filme 'Funk'

♬ Entre os vários documentários sobre ícones da música brasileira que integram a programação do Festival do Rio 2026, um filme de ficção se destaca na mostra Première Brasil.

Trata-se de “Funk”, filme de Aly Muritiba protagonizado por Duda Santos, atriz projetada nacionalmente em novelas como “Garota do momento” (2024 / 2025) e a atual “A nobreza do amor” (2026).

No longa-metragem, que terá as primeiras sessões no Brasil no Festival do Rio, na noite de amanhã, sábado, 3 de outubro, Duda Santos é MC Sabrina, jovem cantora carioca de funk, filha de artista pioneira no gênero, MC Priscila, personagem de MC Nem.

Sabrina vive em conflito com a mãe, com quem mora no Morro dos Prazeres, comunidade carioca situada no bairro de Santa Teresa.

Com elenco que inclui os cantores TZ da Coronel e Lellê, entre outros nomes, o filme “Funk” estreou mundialmente em junho, como parte da programação do Festival de Cinema de Tribeca, realizado em Manhattan (Nova York), nos Estados Unidos.

articles.title: Olivier Martinez Granted Temporary Restraining Order Against Halle Berry, Actress Will Temporarily Have Restricted Visits with Son
articles.summary: The restraining order comes after Martinez alleged that Berry “physically abused” their 12-year-old son, Maceo
articles.body:
A Los Angeles County judge granted a request for a temporary restraining order against Halle Berry filed by her ex-husband, Olivier Martinez, on Oct. 1

In his request for the temporary restraining order, Martinez alleged that Berry had been verbally abusive toward him, and physically abusive toward their 12-year-old son Maceo

The judge declined to bar Berry from contacting Maceo, but did restrict her visitation until an Oct. 16 hearing on the restraining order

Following his allegations that Halle Berry physically abused their 12-year-old son Maceo, Olivier Martinez has been granted a temporary restraining order against the actress.

On Thursday, Oct. 1, a Los Angeles County judge granted Martinez's request for a temporary restraining order that covered both himself and Maceo, according to court records viewed by PEOPLE.

The judge ordered temporarily modified visitation, writing that partial custody is to be "continued to maintain communication between [Berry] and [Maceo], while denying a request that Berry's sobriety be monitored, citing "insufficient information."

The order also modified the hours of Berry's visitation with Maceo to limit her time with him to Mondays and Tuesdays between 10 a.m. and 8 p.m., and Saturdays and Sundays from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

The temporary restraining order will be in effect until a hearing later this month, at which a judge will determine whether or not the order should be made permanent.

In a statement shared with PEOPLE, Berry's attorney Marina Beck described Martinez's filing as "entirely meritless and deliberately misleading."

"To say this filing is entirely meritless and deliberately misleading would be an understatement," Beck said, later adding, "Fortunately, Halle is used to this kind of outrageous conduct from Mr. Martinez and, while she is deeply saddened, she will not allow it to deter her from fighting for Maceo's best interests and providing him with the love and support he needs."

In his Oct. 1 petition, Martinez alleged that Berry, also 60, caused him "emotional and mental distress due to physical abuse of our minor child, Maceo," according to a filing obtained by PEOPLE.

Martinez claimed that Berry "grabbed Maceo by the neck and started choking him while shouting, 'Who is dominant now?! Who is dominant?' " during the alleged incident.

Martinez also claimed in the filing that Berry had previously engaged in "instances of abuse over the course of the last few years," including "additional physical attacks against our son, as well as verbal and emotional abuse from Petitioner to me."

Martinez's lawyer Patrick Baghdaserians said his client's "paramount concern is the health, welfare and the safety of the minor child, hence the action that he took in court by filing the request for domestic violence restraining order. The second concern would be for mother to get the appropriate help that she needs to address her issues so she can better herself, which would in turn help the minor child moving forward." Baghdaserians calls Martinez "a loving parent" who has "tried to do the best he can. Obviously, it's always difficult when you're in a co-parenting relationship. Our paramount concern right now is only one real issue, and that's protecting this great kid."

The temporary restraining order comes three years after Berry and Martinez finalized their divorce in 2023 after a contentious eight-year battle. At the time, Berry was ordered to pay $8,000 a month in child support to Martinez, along with "4.3% of any income she receives above $2,000,000" in additional support.

A hearing on the restraining order is set for Oct. 16.

articles.title: Ajay Devgn on the challenge of making Hindi cinema: How will a Hindi film appeal to everyone?
articles.summary: Ajay Devgn highlights the difficulties of creating Hindi films that resonate with diverse audiences in India, addressing the evolving dynamics of filmmaking at FICCI Frames 2026.
articles.body: At a time when the Hindi film industry is navigating intense competition from international and regional cinema, Ajay Devgn believes making a Hindi film has become one of the toughest challenges for filmmakers.‘Numbers will only follow if you’ve made a good film’Speaking at FICCI Frames 2026, Ajay pointed out that unlike regional cinema, which generally has a clearly defined audience, Hindi films have to cater to viewers with vastly different tastes, languages and sensibilities across the country.”Speaking about the changing dynamics of Hindi cinema, Ajay said, “Today, numbers will only follow if you’ve made a good film; otherwise, you won’t get the numbers. Earlier, the numbers would follow in spite of you not making a great film, but today, the film will crash on the second day.”He continued, “I’m not taking away credit from any other cinema. It is difficult to make films everywhere, whether it is international or traditional cinema. Personally, I feel that making a Hindi film is most difficult because you do not know who your target audience is. When you make a Punjabi, Tamil or Telugu film, you know your audience as it is for a certain region. But for a Hindi film to achieve the numbers, it’s not the same, as every 80 to 90 kms, the language and thought process changes, so if one section of the audience likes the film, the other section might not. How will a Hindi film appeal to everyone? Hence, I feel it is most difficult to write a Hindi film.”‘The core of the original should not be diluted’For Ajay, the success of a sequel isn’t necessarily about recreating the success of the first film — it is about whether audiences have invested enough in the character to want to see more of his story. As he returns as Vijay Salgaonkar in Drishyam: The Conclusion, which hits the theatres this Friday, Ajay said the character cannot be drastically altered simply to create something new. “I think sequels don’t work, the characters work,” he added, pointing to franchises such as Golmaal, Singham and Drishyam as examples where audiences have formed a connection with the central characters.Adding to Ajay’s point, Alok Jain, Head — Hindi & English Entertainment (Streaming, TV & Studios), JioStar, said the challenge for a long-running franchise is to preserve its original DNA while ensuring that its storytelling evolves with its audience. “I think for a 10-year-old franchise, you have to keep building it, keeping in mind that the core of the original is not diluted by any measure,” he said.At the same time, Jain believes a franchise cannot remain frozen in time. He added, “You have to still make that content, which is in sync with the audience, which they want to see now. Because in 10-15 years, things would have changed, emotions and expectations would have changed. You have to do the balancing act.”‘Vijay Salgaonkar is more prepared this time’Explaining how he approached Vijay Salgaokar’s character this time around, Ajay said, “This time, Vijay Salgaonkar is more prepared for what is going to happen. That’s the only difference, otherwise, you can’t digress too much because the film is starting from where it ended. But playing the character now is a bit different because with age, he has also experienced more and developed a certain kind of calmness.”For Ajay, that emotional investment in a character is what allows a franchise to sustain itself. “If you pick up any of these characters, Gopal (Golmaal), Singham (Singham) or Vijay (Drishyam), the audience is invested in them. When the audience is invested in a character, then you can make sequels. You can’t just make a sequel because you have made a great film which worked,” he explained.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Hombres G responde a quienes quieren censurar 'Gilipollas', su nuevo tema: "¿Lo hacemos con Shakespeare o Quevedo? Es absurdo"
articles.standfirst: El grupo compuesto por David Summers, Rafa Gutiérrez, Javier Molina y Dani Mezquita se somete a las cuestiones de Pablo Motos
articles.summary: El grupo compuesto por David Summers, Rafa Gutiérrez, Javier Molina y Dani Mezquita se somete a las cuestiones de Pablo Motos
articles.body: Ha llegado el momento de que ‘El Hormiguero’ ponga el fin a una nueva semana. Tras la visita de David Bisbal, lo hará con la presencia de Hombres G (David Summers, Rafa Gutiérrez, Javier Molina y Dani Mezquita) en su plató. La mítica banda española llega a Antena para presentar su nuevo single 'Gilipollas' y a contar todos los detalles de su gira 2026. Y es que ya lo avisaba Pablo Motos nada más comenzar el programa: “Hoy vamos a pasarlo muy bien”. PABLO MOTOS. En unas pocas horas sale el single ‘Gilipollas’. ¿Va a dar lugar a un nuevo álbum con nuevas canciones? DAVID SUMMERS. Esto arranca con un nuevo disco. Vamos a ir dosificando. El álbum se llama ‘Acojonante’. PABLO MOTOS. He leído que os quieren censurar la palabra ‘Gilipollas’. Os quieren poner un pitido, ¿no? RAFA GUTIÉRREZ. Llevamos usándola toda la vida. Es una expresión normal. De toda la vida. Se ha dicho siempre. Si eres gilipollas, eres gilipollas. No va más allá, como ha sido siempre. La seguiremos usando. DAVID SUMMERS. No creo que lo consigan. Sería muy triste. Cuando íbamos a México, todos estos países eran muy conservadores. Nos censuraban ‘Sufre mamón’. De hace 40 años te estoy hablando. Sería muy triste que en España ocurriese esto, hay que ir hacia adelante, no hacia atrás. JAVIER MOLINA. Censurar el lenguaje de la calle es ridículo. ¿Censuramos a Shakespeare o a Quevedo? Es absurdo, no podemos permitirlo. PABLO MOTOS. En la canción también decís ‘idiota’, ‘imbécil’, ‘caranabo’ y ‘vete con tu madre’. Si os ponen pitos no se va a entender la canción. DAVID SUMMERS. Toda la vida he defendido escribir letras usando el mismo lenguaje coloquial que usamos nosotros. O sea, lo que no se pueden buscar son palabras alternativas. Hombres G siempre lo ha hecho para comunicarnos con nuestro público. Esto es un cachondeo, una broma. PABLO MOTOS. ¿En el mundo de la música hay mucho gilipollas? DAVID SUMMERS. Un montón. Nos dicen mucho lo de que ‘sois muy normales’. La gente espera que si eres artista o famoso seas un gilipollas. Hay muchos. PABLO MOTOS. Yo he oído que en el mundo de los artistas, existe la gilipollez de los lacasitos. ¿La habéis escuchado? RAFA GUTIÉRREZ. No era una gilipollez. La historia real era que tenían un contrato y siempre existían las cláusulas estas pequeñas que no te lees. Entonces ponías, por ejemplo, que sólo haya lacasitos marrones. Y claro, si aceptabas, pensaban que no te habías leído el contrato. Era cierto. JAVIER MOLINA. En el mundo de la farándula, en general, hay mucho gilipollas. Artistas, televisión… Donde hay fama, hay cretinos. Hay muchos tipos de gilipollas. Nosotros hablamos de un déspota, engreído, el que lo sabe todo. De hecho, lo decimos en la canción. No hay que perder el sentido del humor y queremos que España lo tenga. PABLO MOTOS. ¿Cuál sería la prueba definitiva de que alguien es gilipollas? RAFA GUTIÉRREZ. Los que se ofenden cuando les dices gilipollas (ríe). DAVID SUMMERS. Esta canción se puede usar para dedicársela a su gilipollas favorito. Todos tenemos uno, y luego siempre hay cerca alguno. El que se sienta ofendido o aludido, es que es gilipollas. Que tampoco es malo. PABLO MOTOS. Por ejemplo, los que se ponen gafas sin cristal… RAFA GUTIÉRREZ. O los que se ponen la gorra con la visera para atrás. Les da el sol y se ponen la mano. PABLO MOTOS. Oyes esta canción y es como que te desahoga, te quita un peso de encima. ¿Tenéis más de este estilo? DAVID SUMMERS. Es ‘Acojonante’ el disco. Habíamos perdido ese punto canalla nuestro de siempre. He querido hacer un tema cachondo. Hay otros más graciosos. Otro habla satíricamente de las redes sociales. Estoy contento de haber recuperado ese estilo. PABLOS MOTOS. Y las redes sociales y la IA, ¿qué opináis? JAVIER MOLINA. Es cierto que el coeficiente intelectual ha disminuido. Y lo achacan a ver vídeos cortos, mensajes cortos… No pensamos, no leemos un libro. Estamos más mermados mentalmente. Hasta con el GPS. Ahora te va diciendo todo, hasta la casa de tu madre. Todo esto nos hace más estúpidos. DAVID SUMMERS. La gente cree que la IA es un oráculo. La verdad no está ahí, también está manipulada.

articles.title: Bradley Taylor named new Birmingham poet laureate
articles.summary: Bradley Taylor is known for creating instant poems on his typewriter at events and festivals.
articles.body:
Birmingham's new poet laureate has been revealed as Poetry on Demand performer Bradley Taylor.

The 28-year-old said it felt great to take on the two-year role and meant he could "shout and celebrate the city that I love even more than I already do".

Taylor, who was commissioned to write a poem for Peaky Blinders' creator, Steven Knight, has become known for writing poems on-the-spot at festivals, parks and events.

"The city's known for its writing and its poetry, so it's an incredibly important position, because it helps continue celebrating the heritage of Birmingham and its arts, especially in a time when becoming an artist is becoming harder and harder," he said.

He said historically, Birmingham was known for its artists and poetry, from people such as Benjamin Zephaniah, Casey Bailey, and song writers like Ozzy Osbourne and Ruby Turner.

He planned to continue hosting events, working to expand the Zephaniah Forest project across the city , in tribute to the former writer and poet, and support local projects.

"I will also be performing Poetry on Demand with my typewriter across the city over the two-year position," he said.

"I will also be working with Birmingham Libraries to continue celebrating them... while representing the city across the country and doing two nationwide tours."

Taylor started his impromptu poems routine in 2021 and has appeared at the Hay Festival and the Verve Poetry Festival and most recently at International Day of Birmingham.

His read out his Peaky Blinder verse, By Order of the People, at the film's premier in Birmingham in March, celebrating the characters and the city they were from.

Cobain and his then-girlfriend Tracy Marander reportedly paid about $137 for rent and utilities for the apartment. Decades later, fans are paying a few hundred dollars for a single night in the same space.The Airbnb listing also highlights a quiet downtown setting, a queen-sized bed, Wi-Fi, cable and a backyard with a cherry tree. It has received a 4.85-star rating from 95 reviews on the current listing.The house dates back to around 1914Long before Cobain moved in, the building was simply another residential property in Olympia.The Olympia Historical Society and Bigelow House Museum says the house at 114 Pear St NE was erected around 1914. It was designed as a triplex, with two apartments facing the street and a smaller third apartment at the rear.Cobain lived in the building between 1989 and 1991, during a period when Nirvana was developing the music that would eventually take the band far beyond Olympia. The historical society says, according to its sources, that Cobain wrote about 75% of his total lifetime outputwhile living at the property.That history gives the otherwise ordinary-looking building a much bigger place in Nirvana’s story.The wall behind one of Nirvana’s biggest songsThe apartment is also connected to the story behind 'Smells Like Teen Spirit'.According to the Olympia Historical Society, Kathleen Hanna wrote graffiti on the wall of Cobain’s apartment that read “Kurt smells like Teen Spirit.” Cobain later used the phrase as the title of the Nirvana song.The song eventually became one of Nirvana’s best-known tracks and appeared on 'Nevermind', the 1991 album that took the band from the alternative music scene to a much wider audience.That makes the Pear Street apartment more than just a former address. It was part of Cobain’s everyday surroundings during the years when some of the ideas associated with Nirvana’s breakthrough were taking shape.The apartment was there before the fameCobain’s time at the property overlapped with the release of 'Bleach' in 1989 and the period leading up to 'Nevermind'.The difference between the apartment’s appearance and the scale of Nirvana’s eventual success is part of its appeal. There is nothing about the property that suggests it was once connected to one of the most recognizable bands of the grunge era.The building was simply a home for Cobain during a period when he was still developing his career. Soon after, Nirvana’s growing popularity would change the circumstances around him.Today, the apartment gives fans a chance to look back at that earlier chapter rather than only the years when Cobain was already internationally famous.What remains inside the former Cobain homeThe current Airbnb has been decorated around its musical history. The listing mentions original fixtures and memorabilia, while reports have highlighted Nirvana photographs, posters, books and other items connected to Cobain.The Airbnb describes the space as an “eclectic space with musical history” and says it offers a setting for musicians, artists and writers.It remains a small residential studio rather than a formal museum, which gives the stay a different feel. Visitors are not simply looking at memorabilia behind glass; they are staying in a real apartment that was once part of Cobain’s life.For Nirvana fans, that connection is the biggest attraction. The property captures a quieter moment in Cobain’s story, from the years when he was living in Olympia and working on music to the period just before Nirvana’s success changed everything.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Charles Kelley reveals multiple myeloma diagnosis after unexplained rib fractures; Lady A singer plans to keep performing: 'I’m hopeful. I really am'
articles.summary: Charles Kelley of Lady A opens up about his recent multiple myeloma diagnosis following unexpected rib fractures. Despite the shocking news, Kelley expresses hope for his treatment and plans to continue performing with the band. He shares insights on managing his health while staying connected to music and fans.
articles.body: Charles Kelley did not expect a couple of broken ribs to lead to a cancer diagnosis. The Lady A singer, 45, revealed recently that he has multiple myeloma, a rare type of blood cancer. Sitting beside his wife, Cassie Kelley, in a video shared on her Instagram account, the singer explained that doctors started looking more closely at his health after he suffered “a couple random rib fractures.”Those injuries led to several blood tests. One of them eventually gave Kelley an answer he was not expecting. “One of the last blood tests we did, they found a blood cancer in there called multiple myeloma,” he said.The news came as a shock, but Kelley was noticeably focused on what comes next rather than letting the diagnosis take over the conversation. He said he feels healthy and is hopeful about treatment, pointing to how much multiple myeloma care has changed in recent years.What is multiple myeloma?Multiple myeloma is a cancer that begins in plasma cells, a type of white blood cell found in the bone marrow. These cells usually produce antibodies that help the body fight infections. When a person has multiple myeloma, abnormal plasma cells can accumulate in the bone marrow and outnumber the healthy cells that produce red blood cells, platelets and other white blood cells, according to the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.The disease can affect the bones, too. It can cause bone pain or bones that break more easily but an unexplained rib fracture does not mean that someone has multiple myeloma.The condition can also be associated with anaemia, infections, kidney problems and high calcium levels. Some people may have few symptoms when the disease is first detected.Charles Kelley feels hopeful about cancer treatmentDespite the difficult news, Charles Kelley has repeatedly returned to one word: hopeful. “I feel really hopeful, I really do,” he said in the September 29 Instagram video.He also said the treatments for multiple myeloma have “just come so far” over the past five years. A friend who was diagnosed with the same disease a couple of months before Kelley has also been helping him understand what the journey could look like.That personal connection appears to have made the diagnosis feel a little less unfamiliar. Charles Kelley also compared his approach to cancer with the way he previously handled his sobriety journey. He has been open about his struggle with alcohol addiction and marked four years of sobriety in 2026.“In the same spirit of the way we've shared a lot of my sobriety journey just getting this stuff off your chest is so freeing and it takes the power away from it a little bit,” he said.Charles Kelley plans to keep making music during treatmentFor Lady A fans, there is one thing Charles Kelley does not appear ready to put on pause: music. The singer said the band has a new record coming soon and that he expects the first six months of his treatment to be manageable enough for him to continue working.“I can still work,” Kelley said. He acknowledged that there will be difficult days but added that he wants to keep going. Lady A's official tour schedule lists the band's 'This Winter's Night Tour' from December 10 through December 21, 2026. The group will perform in Northfield, Gary, Shipshewana, New York, Bensalem and Greensboro before ending the run with two December 21 shows at Nashville's Ryman Auditorium.For Kelley, staying involved with music is not just about keeping a tour date on the calendar. It is also about holding on to something familiar while life changes around him.A new chapter for the Lady A singerCharles Kelley ended his announcement with the same outlook that ran through the entire conversation. He knows treatment will bring difficult moments, but he does not want to spend all his time thinking about the illness. He and Cassie chose to share the news with fans themselves, just as Kelley has done with other deeply personal parts of his life.“I’m hopeful. I really am,” he said. “We just wanted to let y’all know.”For now, Charles Kelley is looking ahead to treatment, his family, a new Lady A record and the Christmas shows already waiting on the calendar. It is a difficult new chapter, but Kelley seems determined to keep some of his old routine intact — one day, one song and one performance at a time.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer is my childhood podracing dream come true
articles.summary: Star Wars: Galactic Racer takes everything from The Phantom Menace’s brilliant podracing scene and packs it into a thrilling video game.
articles.body: The podracing scene in The Phantom Menace is one of my favorite movie sequences ever. It’s just so dang cool: The futuristic racers tear over treacherous Tatooine terrain while various Star Wars aliens bark at each other in incomprehensible sci-fi languages. Eventually a young Anakin Skywalker proves his mettle by clawing his way from the back of the pack to win the race, which left an impression on me when I first saw it at 10 years old. I always wished I could pilot a podracer myself. Over the past several days, I’ve been able to live out that dream thanks to Star Wars: Galactic Racer, which takes everything from that brilliant scene and packs it into a thrilling video game. In Galactic Racer’s campaign, you play as Shade, a cargo pilot who gets a shot at racing in the underground Galactic League circuit to eventually challenge the smarmy champion Kestar Bool. The game is basically a roguelike. You start a run (called a “tour”) by picking between a few different vehicles — though you don’t get to drive a podracer until partway through the campaign — and selecting various perks that can influence your style of play. Races themselves take place across a few planets, including the desert Jakku planet from The Force Awakens, and you’ll pick different events to participate in from a branching map screen. After each race, you’ll get rewards to help craft your build, and along the way, you’ll also play brief sections where you walk around as Shade, talk with other characters, and upgrade your vehicle. [Image: This is Shade, the customizable player character. Characters make fun of their helmet, which I always found funny. It’s all standard roguelike stuff, but the familiar format lets me better focus on the races themselves, which are really intense. Turns and obstacles that look far away come up in the blink of an eye, forcing you to react in an instant. Two different kinds of boosts mean you’re constantly surging forward in some way. And all the while, other racers are on the hunt, often ramming your craft or targeting you with weapons. I nearly always felt like I was just on the cusp of losing control, and a split-second mistake usually results in a crash. (When you crash, the whole game also briefly stops to showcase your wreckage flying across the track, which is satisfying in its own way.) Things get even more intense when you finally get into an actual podracer. It’s extreme in the way that I imagined racing a vehicle in the Star Wars universe would actually be. There’s more to that feeling than the races themselves, though as developer Fuse Games — a relatively new studio with former staffers of Need for Speed, Burnout, and Star Wars Battlefront maker Criterion Games — makes the whole experience feel authentically Star Wars. The speeders and vehicles are grungy and worn, and your fellow racers constantly bicker at each other. (You’ll hear a lot of Huttese.) There are wipe transitions between scenes and bombastic, John Williams-esque music. My favorite touch might be the brief scene before each race where you press different buttons to prepare your vehicle, like what the racers do in The Phantom Menace. [Image: Many races force you to drive through cramped caverns, which can be terrifying at high speeds. That intensity also means that the campaign can be frustrating. I crashed a lot, often because I couldn’t see an obstacle in front of me until far too late, and the opposing racers can be extremely aggressive. I sometimes wished I actually had the reflexes of a Jedi to be able to keep up. A run can take a long time — late in the game, they can exceed two hours — which makes a late loss exasperating. Between tours, you can permanently boost your vehicle’s stats to make the next run easier, though that wasn’t always enough to make the pain of a loss worth it. Occasionally, I turned down the difficulty so that I could play without as much pressure. Even after a brutal tour, though, I kept finding myself thinking about when I could carve out the time for another run. Galactic Racer isn’t the first Star Wars racing title, but it feels like the best realization yet of a game that embodies what made The Phantom Menace’s racing scene so memorable. I know I’ll never actually get to pilot a podracer, but Galactic Racer is close enough for me to live out my childhood dream. Star Wars: Galactic Racer launches on October 6th on PC, PS5, and Xbox.

articles.title: Sylvester Stallone showered in his clothes to survive before ‘Rocky’ fame
articles.summary: Sylvester Stallone's memoir "The Steps" reveals how he survived on raw eggs and cottage cheese in a tiny New York City apartment before "Rocky" fame.
articles.body: Before Sylvester Stallone became one of Hollywood's biggest stars, he had just $60 to his name — with $43.60 already set aside for rent. But even as he struggled to make ends meet in New York City, the future "Rocky" icon refused to give up on his dream. In his new memoir, "The Steps," Stallone recounts the years before fame, including his arrival in New York City in 1969, determined to become an actor despite poverty, rejection and uncertainty. The 80-year-old told Fox News Digital that even in his darkest moments, he held on to the belief that his life would eventually change for the better. "I think it comes from naïveté and the folly of youth, that you still have this sense of, 'I can do it, I can break the mold,'" Stallone said. "I hadn't been beaten enough by life yet to say it's over because, as an actor, if you haven't made it by 30, I'd say 99% you're never going to make it. I wasn't aware of that, so I kept going." "In New York, when I was really down and out, I didn't focus on, 'God, you're going to be destitute,'" Stallone said. "There was this certain optimism that if you put every effort forward, if you denied yourself every moment of pleasure of going to the movies, dating a girl — if you abandoned all that and dedicate yourself, I believe that you'll know 100% whether you actually have a chance to be this character you always wished you could be." Stallone never stopped believing he would one day make it as an actor. WATCH: SYLVESTER STALLONE REFLECTS ON CHILDHOOD TRAUMA, ‘ROCKY’ AND WHY ‘TRYING’ MATTERS MOST After leaving the American College in Switzerland without graduating and dropping out of the University of Miami just a few credits shy of a drama degree, Stallone returned to New York City with little to his name. He rented a room so cramped that he later compared it to the minimum size recommended for a federal jail cell. He shared a bathroom with 10 other people. Stallone also found work as an usher at a movie theater, earning just $34 a week. He said the job became an education in filmmaking. Night after night, he studied the movies he watched, keeping his dream alive. Stallone said he would shower with his clothes on to save money on laundry. If he were lucky enough to find a bar of soap that didn't have a "strange hair" stuck to it, he would use it to lather up "my shirt, pants, underwear, socks — and myself." "I could never afford to go to a laundromat," Stallone said. "My wife thinks this is so gross, 'Why would you take a shower with your clothes on?' I said, 'It made sense to me at the time, rather than going down to the laundromat. But this was a tenement home. It was so bad. But you do what you could to survive.'" To stave off hunger, Stallone would eat spoonfuls of cottage cheese, then down three or four raw eggs. In the book, he recalled later treating himself to chicken breast and apple juice. "It's the only thing that made sense numerically, financially," he said. "Of course, it's all wrong. It's terrible. I'm surprised I didn't get salmonella, really. It's really quite remarkable. But these two things at a certain time of year, because in the summer, the cottage cheese would rot, and the eggs would spoil. And at the time, I just thought it was so convenient. No dishes. You drink the egg, so you don't have to wash anything. You didn't need a fork. And the cottage cheese, it's a spoon, and you throw the cup away." Stallone wrote in the book, "I wouldn't recommend this diet to anyone. But if you're young and poor, it will suffice, which is why I used eating raw eggs in 'Rocky' to give some insight into Rocky's ways of approaching his life." Stallone had a dollar or two a day for food. He needed a job, and fast. One of Stallone's earliest gigs was cleaning the lion cages at Central Park Zoo. The smell was bad enough — but it wasn't what frightened him. "I also feared for my life," he wrote. "The lions were always close by, always watching. They looked through me. They were behind a set of bars, but that didn't stop the great sad creatures from wedging their huge snouts between the bars to sniff me out. The way they inhaled and exhaled made an eerie moaning sound, like they already knew what I was going to taste like." During that period, Stallone faced repeated rejection from agents, including one who criticized his deep voice and asymmetrical mouth — two traits that would later become signatures of his screen persona. While he was able to save enough money for a coat to brave the city's bitter winter, it's one gig he doesn't miss. "Every customer gets cranky over this and that, 'Hey, there's not enough coleslaw here. This sandwich should weigh an ounce and a half more,'" Stallone said with a laugh. "You'd be shocked. I learned to be a really good fish cutter, like for lox on bagels. I still would hear, 'I can't see through the salmon.' They wanted the cut so thin that you could actually see light. Oh man. And you're cutting your fingers off, too." "And then the characters that come in at two in the morning, the outrageous drunks and gangsters, unbelievable," Stallone continued. "You'd be shocked who walks into a place at two in the morning and wants a sandwich. So that's colorful. And of course, I ended up in jail, but that's only because of the stupid deli." "I thought I was living OK, a decent life," he said. "But by today's standards, you were on the cusp of oblivion." After an altercation at the deli, Stallone found himself handcuffed in the back of a police car, still wearing his apron and name tag. He was sent to "The Tombs," New York's notoriously violent detention facility — or, as Stallone put it, "the place of nightmares." He was put into a 20-foot-by-20-foot holding cell with at least 25 other men. One man was already pounding another's head into a small hole that prisoners used as a toilet. A criminal court judge eventually released Stallone. "If you don't sacrifice completely and fail, you'll suffer for the rest of your life going, 'Why didn't I try harder? Why didn't I use whatever God-given talent I had to be the absolute best?'" Stallone said. "If you fail, you can say, 'I tried.' People can never point a finger in your face and say, 'You didn't try hard enough.'
